newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FEATURE - Industrial city harbours claim to rule Ukraine.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Industrial city harbours claim to rule Ukraine.

text.p: A disc jockey joked during a recent chat show that this Ukrainian industrial city not only regularly produces national leaders but some pretty good singers and musicians too.
He was not far off. At least on the national leaders.
Dnipropetrovsk, in eastern Ukraine, has been home to a long line of Communist Party bosses and now to leaders of post-Soviet Ukraine.

Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev started his political career here and in the nearby satellite city of Dniprodzerzhinsk. Another native son was Vladimir Shcherbitsky, Soviet Ukraine's hardline Communist Party ruler for 17 years.
Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma launched his career in the area as director of Yuzhmash, the world's largest missile plant.
Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko is from Dnipropetrovsk, as are several ministers and some 200 officials -- from the general prosecutor to the head of state television's news programmes.
"It's a big, even a huge problem. You can't even imagine the scale of the problem," said a senior Kuchma aide.
"We are trying to change this scenario, to establish a regional balance, but it's not an easy task. This is potentially explosive for the country."
Olexander Razumkov, director of Kiev's Independent Centre for Economic and Political Studies, said many Ukrainian appointments were based on personal loyalty rather than professional qualifications.
"It's dangerous and it's unnatural for civilised, democratic countries," he said.
Ukraine's average wage is around $80 a month, but Dnipropetrovsk has far more luxury cars than the capital Kiev.
Its newly-renovated airport could have been transplanted from the West.
Some newspapers see the city as a Ukrainian Frankfurt, drawing parallels between Germany's financial capital and powerful Dnipropetrovsk-based banks.

"It's a good idea to transfer capital from Kiev to Dnipropetrovsk," the daily Ukraina-Centre wrote recently. "It should be done from economic, political and cultural standpoints, and even to strengthen Ukrainian statehood."
Analysts say there are four main financial-industrial centres in Ukraine. Dnipropetrovsk heads the list, followed by coal-rich Donetsk, another major export base.
Kiev takes third place, followed by the southern region around the Black Sea port of Odessa.
Dnipropetrovsk is the centre for Ukraine's metallurgical sector, which brings in almost half the country's hard currency, while local energy and chemical firms are also important.

The skyline of the Soviet-built city on the Dnieper river is dominated with smokestacks. But posh shops and offices have opened in the centre in the last year and banks have started moving to luxuriously renovated offices.
Local trader United Energy Systems (UES) buys up almost half of Ukraine's gas imports, one of several monopolist trading firms with strong influence on the economy as a whole.

"Through this energy they (the traders) control much of the country's economy, if not all of it," said Hanna Lyuta, Ukraine's leading oil and gas commentator. "We're talking not only about gas but also about electricity, pipe production, industry, metallurgy and so on.
"These traders have already become a state within a state. Don't bother asking why Ukraine imports so much gas."

Sources at the State Oil and Gas Committee said Ukraine, which imports 66 billion cubic metres of gas a year from Russia and Turkmenistan, has some 10 billion cubic metres in storage. Domestic output is around 18.2 billion cubic metres a year.
"The choice of traders was not accidental. They pushed their way in with arguments, scandals and threats," said Oleh Dorozhovets, deputy editor of the Oil & Gas Bulletin.
"UES fortunes have increased simultaneously with the current leadership."
But UES president Yulia Tymoshenko denied the firm had any special treatment from the government.
"Gas trading is a very serious marathon. Only a few companies have survived this difficult market race," she said.
Ukraine, independent for five years, still lacks strong political parties and a stable multi-partial system, and some commentators say clanlike political structures are to blame.

"Ukraine's political structure still is not exactly of the clan type, but it is on its way. The interests of the first person (the president) and the second one (the prime minister) do not necessarily dovetail," said Razumkov.
"Inside the Dnipropetrovsk group there is a harsh rivalry -- although it's going on under the table."
The political magazine Demos, discussing reports of top-level corruption, drew parallels with countries in Africa and Latin America.

"The evolution of governmental authority in Ukraine, its "criminalisation' over the last few years, closely resembles the situation in many African or Latin American countries some time ago," the magazine said.
"Over past centuries the ruling elites in Ukraine had an atrophied sense of statehood, or even of nationhood.
"They viewed the possibility to serve in either the Lithuanian, Polish or Russian govermental structures as an opportunity to improve their own material well-being."
